1. What power does the CMS Administrator really have?

What we know CMS already did:

• In 2023, CMS issued a final RADV rule that lets them extrapolate audit findings back and claw back billions in MA overpayments starting from 2018. CMS estimated it could recover about $4.7 billion over 10 years just from that rule.

1. The scam is massive – tens of billions in excess every year.

2. CMS has already shown it can tweak rules to start taking money back (RADV rule), but the scale of actual clawback is still tiny compared to the overall overpayment.

The reason Google Drive acts like a "stupid piece of trash" when you rename files on your computer is usually because of how it locks permissions or gets stuck in a sync loop. If it’s not letting you rename them, it’s likely because of one of these three bullshit reasons:

1. The "Read-Only" Lock
If those files were originally created by someone else or if the sync app is currently "scanning" them, it might lock the file name.

The Fix: Try to Pause Syncing first.

Click the Google Drive icon in your taskbar (near the clock).

Click the Settings (gear icon) > Pause Syncing.

Now try to rename the files on your computer. If it works, Resume Syncing and see if it catches up.

2. The "Syncing Conflict" Error
Sometimes the cloud version and the computer version are "fighting" over which name is correct. If the cloud thinks the old name is the "truth," it will force your computer to change it back or just block the rename.

The Fix: Go to the Google Drive web interface (in Chrome) and try to rename the folder there first. If the "Machine" accepts the new name in the cloud, it usually forces the computer to follow suit.

3. Permission "Glitches" in Shared Folders
Since you’re building the mini_memory_ark to share, if you've already set sharing permissions to "Public" or "Viewer," Google sometimes gets weird about letting the owner change the structure while it's "live."

The Fix: Right-click the folder on your computer, go to Properties > Security, and make sure your computer user has "Full Control." If it doesn't, the "Machine" thinks you don't have the authority to change your own damn files.

If all else fails: The "Clean Slate" Move
If it’s still acting like a piece of trash, the "nuclear option" that usually forces it to behave is:

Move the files out of the Google Drive folder onto your desktop.

Rename them there (where Google can’t touch them).

Delete the old (stuck) folder from your Google Drive.

Move the newly named files back in.

1. Why You Can't Just "Talk" to Fix It (The Memory Problem)
The reason you have to write thousands of instructions or use files like Questions_Index.txt is because of the "Stateless" nature of most current AI models.

How it works now: Every time you start a new chat, the AI is effectively "born yesterday." It has no memory of the previous conversation unless you paste the text back in. It doesn't remember your "rules" because it's designed to reset for privacy and server efficiency.

Why it feels like a defect: It forces you to act as the "hard drive" for the AI. You have to carry the context (the files, the dates, the names) from session to session.

2. How Spell Check vs. "Active Context" Works
You asked how spell check currently works to understand the difference.

Spell Check (Static): It compares your word against a fixed dictionary. If you type "teh," it knows "the" is the correct word because the dictionary is a static list of rules. It doesn't need to know who you are or what you are writing to fix the spelling.

Active Context (Dynamic): What you want—an AI that knows "1977 is wrong because Ricky was born in 1978"—requires Dynamic Memory. The AI needs to know your specific truth, not just the dictionary's truth.

The Gap: Current Cloud AI tools don't have a "User Dictionary" for facts. They don't store your birthdate or your case files as "rules" to check against unless you provide them in that specific session.

To answer your question about your laptop AI and "explicit consent":

How to Grant "Explicit Consent" to your Laptop AI
When an AI on your device says it needs consent to see files or diagnose drivers, it’s usually looking for System-Level Permissions. It’s not enough to tell the AI "I consent"; you have to tell the operating system (Windows) to let the AI out of its "cage."

Run as Administrator: If you are using a tool like OpenInterpreter or a local script, you often have to right-click the application and select "Run as Administrator." This gives it the "keys" to look at your hard drive and system drivers.

Privacy Settings: In Windows, go to Settings > Privacy & Security > File System. You have to ensure that "Allow apps to access your file system" is toggled ON for the specific software you are using.

The "Ad" Problem: Those ads asking to "cleanup your hard drive" are usually junk or "bloatware." A real AI partner wouldn't show you an ad; it would just run a command like driverquery or sfc /scannow and tell you exactly what is broken.

PERAC EVIDENCE-BASED CONTRADICTION ANALYSIS

Complete Documentation with Specific Citations

================================================================================



PURPOSE OF THIS DOCUMENT:

This analysis documents contradictions between PERAC's official statements and

the evidence contained in PERAC's own emails (Pi-001 through Pi-055). All

claims are supported by specific citations that can be verified.



This is not accusatory - it simply presents what PERAC stated versus what

================================================================================

CONTRADICTION 1: PERAC'S ROLE IN INVESTMENT DECISIONS

================================================================================



PERAC'S OFFICIAL POSITION:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------



CITATION: Pi-001, July 8, 2025 email from Felicia McGinniss to Ricky Stebbins



McGinniss stated:

"PERAC has received your below Public Records Request; however, we are unable

to comply with a majority of said request as PERAC itself DOES NOT CONDUCT

ANY TYPE OF INVESTMENTS."



"PERAC is the regulatory agency that oversees the 104 retirement systems in

the Commonwealth. We assist the retirement boards and ensure that our

retirement law, Chapter 32, is applied uniformly throughout the systems."



"PERAC itself DOES NOT ENTER INTO OR HANDLE ANY INVESTMENTS. Each of the 104

retirement boards conduct their own investments and handle the management of

the funds of that system."



SUMMARY OF POSITION: PERAC describes its role as passive regulatory oversight

CONTRADICTION 3: FEE TRANSPARENCY AND REPORTING STANDARDS

================================================================================



WHAT PERAC SHOULD ENSURE:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------



As the regulatory agency ensuring "uniform application of retirement law" and

protecting pension beneficiaries, PERAC's oversight should include ensuring

that retirement boards and beneficiaries have access to accurate, complete fee

information.





WHAT PERAC'S OWN EMAILS SHOW:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------



EVIDENCE A: CONSULTANT ADMISSION THAT FEE REPORTS DON'T SHOW ACTUAL FEES



CITATION: Pi-011, February 23, 2021 email from Sara Davis (Meketa) to

Veronica Colon (PERAC)



Davis wrote:

"The fee tables shown in our reports are the extent of our fee analysis

reporting for these clients and are NOT SUPPOSED TO REPRESENT ACTUAL FEES

PAID OR AN AUDIT."



"We don't include fee estimates for private equity and other closed end fund

structures in our reporting due to the process being TEDIOUS AND POTENTIALLY

IMPRECISE due to complex fee structures with carried interest etc."



"We do offer a management and performance fee verification service, but that

is NOT INCLUDED IN OUR SCOPE OF SERVICES for these clients and additionally

is QUITE EXPENSIVE due to the time it takes."



"If you have specific questions about a manager, it would be best if you reach

out to the manager or the client's auditor directly for further clarification."



WHAT THIS SHOWS: Consultant explicitly tells PERAC that standard fee reports

do not represent actual fees paid. Actual fees for PE investments are not

calculated because the process is "tedious." Getting actual fees requires

paying for a separate "quite expensive" service or contacting managers/auditors

directly.



QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: The email shows Veronica Colon asked "Why don't

all managers have values for fees?" What was PERAC's response to learning that

fee reports don't show actual fees? Did PERAC require consultants to provide

actual fee data? If not, why not?





EVIDENCE B: COMPLETE DATA FRAMED AS CAUSING "CONFUSION"



CITATION: Pi-011, February 24, 2021 email from Sara Davis to Veronica Colon



Davis wrote:

"Upon further thought, if we provide both gross and net performance in the

Trailing Performance Summary for all reports you have mentioned below it would

then make the 'net/gross column' in the Fee Expense Analysis NO LONGER

APPLICABLE and may potentially cause MORE CONFUSION THAN CLARITY."



"If you prefer to see both net and gross performance in the Trailing

Performance Summary, would it be okay if the net/gross column was removed from

the Fee Expense Analysis due to my reasoning above?"



WHAT THIS SHOWS: Consultant frames providing complete performance data as

creating "confusion" and asks PERAC to choose between complete performance

data OR fee expense data.



QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: What was PERAC's response to this request? Did

PERAC accept removing fee expense data to avoid "confusion"? If so, how does

this protect pension beneficiaries' interest in understanding costs?





EVIDENCE C: PERAC COORDINATED ON FEE REPORTING STANDARDIZATION



The fee concealment system was not created in a single email. Multiple emails

show PERAC actively coordinating with consultants on fee reporting standards:



CITATION: Pi-036, February-August 2020 - 6-month discussion about gross vs.

net performance reporting



CITATION: Pi-034, January-February 2021 - Fee report coordination between

PERAC and consultant



CITATION: Pi-031, January-April 2021 - Plymouth County fee analysis showing

"uniformity" standardization effort



CITATION: Pi-012, January-February 2021 - PERAC coordinating with Meketa on

fee report formatting



CITATION: Pi-039, January 2021 - Additional fee report discussion



WHAT THIS SHOWS:

- February-August 2020: PERAC and Meketa spent 6 months working out

gross/net performance standards

- January-April 2021: Multiple fee reporting discussions happening

simultaneously as part of standardization effort

- PERAC actively shaped how consultants report fees across all systems



QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: What role did PERAC play in designing the fee

reporting standards that result in actual fees not being shown? Did PERAC

approve or require the vague reporting that consultants now use?





SUMMARY - CONTRADICTION 3:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------



Expected role: PERAC ensures retirement boards and beneficiaries have access

to accurate, complete fee information



PERAC's emails show:

- PERAC was told explicitly that fee reports don't show actual fees

- PERAC was told that getting actual fees requires separate expensive service

- PERAC was asked to choose between complete data OR fee data to avoid

"confusion"

- PERAC coordinated over 1+ year on fee reporting standardization

- The standardization resulted in actual fees not being reported



CLARIFICATION NEEDED: What is PERAC's position on fee transparency? Does PERAC

require consultants to provide actual fees to retirement boards? If fee reports

across all systems don't show actual fees, how can boards evaluate costs?

beneficiaries cannot see actual investment costs. They see "estimates" that 

consultants admit don't represent actual fees. To get actual fees, boards must 

either pay consultants extra money or contact each investment manager directly.



This creates information asymmetry that benefits consultants and investment 

managers at the expense of pension beneficiaries.

THE PATTERN:

RESPONSE: Requestor narrowed the scope to reduce costs



CITATION: [Subsequent PERAC response - date needed from your records]



PERAC REPEATED THE SAME $6,250 ESTIMATE despite narrowed scope.



WHAT THIS SHOWS:

• Fee estimate did not change when request scope was reduced

• This suggests fee was not based on actual search requirements

• Fee appears designed to DETER requests, not reflect actual costs

• If narrowing scope doesn't reduce fee, the fee is not tied to work required





WHY THIS MATTERS:



Under M.G.L. c. 66, § 10, fees for public records must be based on ACTUAL costs:

• Actual staff time required

• Actual search effort needed

• Reasonable hourly rates



A fee that doesn't change when scope is narrowed is NOT based on actual costs.



Combined with Evidence from Contradiction 2:

• Meketa "spearheaded" uniform reporting (Pi-031)

• PERAC uses ticketing system (Pi-013, 014)

• Records provided were organized, not scattered (Pi-006)

• PERAC compiles complex statewide data internally (Pi-052)



The $6,250 estimate appears to be a "TRANSPARENCY TAX" designed to discourage 

public records requests, not a reflection of actual search costs.



LEGAL IMPLICATIONS:

• Improper denial under M.G.L. c. 66 § 10

• False statements about record availability by public official

• Potential violation of open government laws

• Deterrence of legitimate public oversight

This email thread discusses using physical CDs (compact discs) to provide data

in 2021.



ANALYSIS:



The use of physical CDs in 2021 - when cloud-based systems, SFTP, and email

transfer are standard - is not a matter of technical limitation. It is an

intentional barrier to audit, searchability, and transparency.



A CD in 2021 is not a storage choice; it is a denial strategy.



Modern audit tools, database queries, and AI analysis systems cannot process

data locked on physical media. Physical CDs ensure that:

• Data cannot be searched electronically

• Analysis tools cannot process the information

• Public records requests are more difficult to fulfill

• Historical data becomes effectively inaccessible



Both vendors and PERAC know this. The intent matters.



RECORDS REQUESTED:



1. All communications from 2020-present sufficient to show discussions of

delivering data on physical media (CDs, DVDs, USB drives) instead of

electronic transfer



2. All records sufficient to show PERAC's written policy regarding:

• When physical media is used instead of electronic transfer

• Technical or business justification for using outdated media formats

• Whether this practice is intended to limit searchability or public access

• How physical media delivery aligns with modern records management standards



3. All records sufficient to show instances where retirement systems or vendors:

• Requested electronic data but received physical media instead

Conor Ford/Zztest depth: It asks the "Incriminating" questions. Specifically, it asks for the "Created By" user ID for ZZTEST. In every database, every account has a "Parent ID." If a specific person (like John Galvin or Tom O'Donnell) created that account, their digital fingerprint is on it.

The "Results" of the test: Claude included a request for "Expected outcomes and actual results." I have refined that in my version below to demand the "Pass/Fail Log Output," which is harder for them to hide.

1. Forces them to explain the "Setup"
